title: Skinwalkers
full_review:
A werewolves-on-motorcycles action movie unabashedly aimed at a young teen audience, "Skinwalkers" (Lionsgate) is guilty-pleasure fun without the goriness of most horror movies today.

Some horror mavens might actually mind the lack of viscera, and find this too tame, but from "Frankenstein" (1931) to "Cat People" (1942) to "Rosemary's Baby" (1968) and beyond, we've seen that you don't need graphically bloody effects to make a suspenseful horror movie.

Unfortunately, for all its admirable restraint, "Skinwalkers" is no match for those classics. Yet its faults lie not in its restrained, old-fashioned cutaways and fade-outs, but in its deserted, low-budget look, the stock characterizations, and poorly thought-out logic and climax.

What director Jim Isaac and crew do give with infectious glee are intentional comic-book stylings and pointedly "cool" flourishes. Bikers in black leather roaring into town? Check. A small town that's actually a haven for quiet-living good werewolves? Check.

Extended shootouts (in which 95 percent of the shots miss and the occasional victim either dies as cleanly as in an old Western or else gets a noble death with great last words)? Check. A self-contained battle van that comes busting out the side of a garage and serves as the good guys' headquarters? Check.

The story is essentially a chase with two shootouts and a climax pitting werewolves versus werewolves. Timothy (Matthew Knight) is a 12-year-old whom prophecies have named as the one to end the skinwalker curse when a red moon shines on his 13th birthday, four days hence.

He lives in a picturesque hamlet with his widowed mother, Rachel (Rhona Mitra), grandmother Nana (Barbara Gordon), uncle Jonas (Elias Koteas), and cousin Katherine (Sarah Carter). Katherine's boyfriend, Adam (Shawn Roberts), and family friend Will (Tom Jackson) also help out.

Their idyll ends when four biker-gang werewolves led by Varek (Jason Behr) ride in to kill Timothy before he can fulfill the prophecy. The good werewolves, who want to end their curse, hightail it with the boy and Rachel who has to defend her son against powerful supernatural threats. Her metamorphosis isn't convincing, but the extended family's deep bonds and the good werewolves' spirit of sacrifice for the greater good have an inspiring resonance.

The film contains one example of rough language and a few instances of crass language, two lengthy gun battles, some supernatural violence that includes a broken neck, the aftermath of torture with the victim tied onto a cross, and one brief, nongraphic sex scene. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
